1 
 
June 15, 2026 
 
Dr. Mehmet Oz 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
United States Department of Health and Human Services  
Attention: CMS-9898-NC 
P.O. Box 8016, Baltimore, MD 21244-8016 
 
Assistant Secretary Thomas Keane, M.D. 
Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC) 
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services 
330 C Street, SW, Floor 7 
Washington, DC 20201 
 
Re: Interoperability Standards & Prior Authorization (PA) for Drugs (0062-P) 
 
Dear Dr. Oz and Assistant Secretary Keane: 
 
The Association for Behavioral Health and Wellness (ABHW) appreciates the opportunity to 
submit comments to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) and the Office of the 
National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC) on Interoperability Standards 
and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule.  
 
ABHW is the national voice for payers managing behavioral health insurance benefits. Our 
member companies provide coverage to 200 million people in both the public and private 
sectors to treat mental health (MH), substance use disorders (SUDs), and other behaviors that 
impact health and wellness. Our organization aims to increase access, drive integration, 
support prevention, raise awareness, reduce stigma, and advance evidence-based treatment 
and quality outcomes. Furthermore, our policy work aims to ensure that physical and 
behavioral health care is integrated and coordinated. ABHW is committed to ensuring better 
outcomes for whole-person care for all individuals and communities. We believe access to 
comprehensive, evidence-based MH and SUD services is critical to enhancing patientsâ€™ health 
and overall well-being. 
 
ABHW supports CMS's goal of improving timely access to medications and streamlining the 
prior authorization process and making electronic prior authorization more available.  
1. Improving Communications and Decision Timeframes for Prior Authorizations 
CMS proposes to revise prior authorization decision timeframes across Medicare Advantage 
(MA), Medicaid, CHIP, and Marketplace plans, generally aligning drug prior authorization 
requests with the timelines established under the Interoperability and Prior Authorization Rule 
(CMS-0057-F). This proposed rule would shorten standard review timeframes in several 
programs, including reducing Medicaid, CHIP, and Marketplace standard drug prior 
authorization decisions to 24 hours or 7 calendar days, depending on the program, while 
 
2 
 
establishing expedited review timeframes of 72 hours for most drug requests and 24 hours for 
expedited requests in Marketplace plans.  
The proposed turnaround times do not adequately account for the clinical and operational 
complexity of pharmacy prior authorizations. Unlike many medical prior authorization 
requests, pharmacy reviews often involve dosage and quantity limits, step therapy 
requirements, site-of-care considerations, diagnosis-specific criteria, and coordination across 
pharmacy and medical benefits. Many requests also require additional clinical documentation, 
such as chart notes, laboratory results, treatment history, or confirmation of prior medication 
use. 
As a result of these shortened turnaround times, health plans may be forced to deny 
incomplete requests rather than make clinically appropriate coverage determinations. This 
could increase denials, appeals, and administrative burden for providers and plans, ultimately 
delaying patient access to care, an outcome that is inconsistent with CMS's goals. 
In addition, implementing these requirements will require significant system changes, 
workflow redesign, and technology investments across health plans, pharmacy benefit 
managers, and provider-facing platforms. Given the volume and complexity of pharmacy prior 
authorization requests, operationalizing these requirements will be challenging. 
ABHW recommends that CMS allow health plans to pause applicable turnaround 
time requirements when additional clinically necessary information has been 
requested but not yet received from the provider. Allowing plans to "stop the 
clock" in these circumstances would support more accurate and clinically 
appropriate determinations, reduce avoidable denials and appeals, and better 
align the policy with CMS's goal of improving patient access to needed 
medications. 
Exception for Bundled Payments  
Some affected payers, including behavioral health (BH) Medicaid Managed Care Organizations 
(MCOs), manage only behavioral health and substance use disorder (SUD) benefits and do not 
administer medical or pharmacy benefits. These plans often cover Medication-Assisted 
Treatment (MAT), such as methadone treatment, through bundled case rates that include the 
medication, administration of the medication, counseling, assessments, laboratory services, 
and other related treatment components. It is unclear how these bundled services should be 
categorized under the proposed rule. Separating the medication component from the 
associated behavioral health services would be operationally challenging and may create 
significant reporting and documentation burdens. 
We recommend that bundled behavioral health and SUD treatment services that 
include medications be exempt from the proposed 24-hour turnaround time for 
drugs and instead be subject to the prior authorization timeliness standards for 
 
3 
 
non-drug items and services (7 calendar days standard / 72 hours expedited). 
Because these bundled services include a range of clinical services beyond the 
medication itself, CMS should clarify in the final rule that they are processed 
through the Prior Authorization API for non-drug items and services, rather than 
through the National Council for Prescription Drug Programs (NCPDP) 
standards used for pharmacy benefits. In addition, applying the non-drug authorization 
timeframes would provide plans with sufficient time to verify the credentials of out-of-network 
providers seeking to furnish these services. Credentialing reviews are often necessary to ensure 
providers meet state Medicaid program requirements and cannot reasonably be completed 
within 24 hours. The proposed drug-related turnaround time does not account for these 
operational requirements and could create compliance challenges while undermining program 
integrity safeguards. 
As an example, Louisiana Medicaid reimburses opioid treatment programs (OTPs) through a 
bundled payment for HCPCS code H0020 that includes a broad range of services, such as 
methadone medication dosing and dispensing, counseling, urine drug testing, physician 
examinations, evaluation and management visits, care coordination, and laboratory services. 
Given the multiple clinical and administrative components included within a single bundled 
payment, it is unclear how the proposed prior authorization turnaround time requirements 
would be operationalized and measured.  
2. Reporting Usage Metrics for Patient Access, Provider Access, Payer-to-Payer, 
and Prior Authorization APIs 
ABHW has concerns about the scope of the proposed Payer-to-Payer API requirements and the 
potential for broad sharing of sensitive health information between health plans. While we 
support efforts to improve care coordination and reduce administrative burden, the exchange 
of structured and unstructured clinical documentation may result in the disclosure of 
information that is not necessary to support continuity of care, particularly when there is no 
active transition between health plans. This concern is especially significant for behavioral 
health information, which may be subject to heightened privacy protections under 42 CFR Part 
2 (Part 2) that has unique confidentiality requirements. 
We encourage CMS to limit payer-to-payer data exchange to situations in which a 
member is actively transitioning between health plans and the information is 
needed to support continuity of care. CMS should also require explicit member 
authorization before information is shared and ensure that exchanged data are 
limited to the minimum necessary to support care coordination and coverage 
determinations. Rather than requiring the transmission of full clinical 
documentation, CMS should adopt a more targeted approach that balances 
interoperability goals with patient privacy and confidentiality protections. 
3. RFI on Streamlining Step Therapy Through Technology and Data Sharing 
 
4 
 
ABHW appreciates CMS's interest in exploring how interoperability and data sharing can 
improve the efficiency and transparency of utilization management processes, including step 
therapy. Enhanced access to historical claims data could be particularly valuable when 
individuals transition to a new health plan, reducing the need for providers to resubmit records 
and helping avoid unnecessary repetition of previously completed therapies. 
Many health plans already use automated adjudication tools and historical claims lookback 
capabilities to support step therapy administration. In addition, step therapy criteria 
appropriately vary across payers based on differences in clinical policies, formularies, and 
benefit designs. Existing transition-of-care processes, including grandfathering and override 
mechanisms, also help ensure continuity of care for established therapies. 
ABHW recommends that CMS support the targeted use of historical claims data 
to inform step therapy decisions, particularly for new members, while preserving 
payer flexibility to apply plan-specific clinical criteria. CMS should avoid policies 
that would require health plans to automatically accept step therapy 
determinations made by other payers. 
 
 
 
 
                          ***** 
ABHW is ready to support CMS and ONC in efforts to modernize health IT infrastructure, 
improve interoperability, and reduce unnecessary administrative burden. 
We look forward to working with you to advance interoperability and improve behavioral 
health outcomes nationwide. Please contact Kathryn Cohen, Senior Director of Regulatory 
Affairs at cohen@abhw.org, if you have any questions.  
 
Sincerely,  
 
Debbie Witchey, MHA  
President and CE

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Association for Behavioral Health and Wellness (ABHW); signed by Debbie Witchey, MHA, President and CEO
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association; Payer association
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** ABHW represents payers managing behavioral health insurance benefits for 200 million people in public and private sectors; focuses on mental health, substance use disorders, integration, prevention, and evidence-based treatment.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

ABHW supports CMS's goals of improving medication access, streamlining PA, and expanding electronic prior authorization, but requests modifications to account for pharmacy PA complexity, bundled behavioral health/SUD services, payer-to-payer privacy risks, and plan-specific step therapy criteria. The comment recommends a stop-the-clock policy for incomplete requests, an exemption for bundled MAT services from 24-hour drug PA timeframes, tighter limits and authorization requirements for payer-to-payer data exchange, and targeted use of historical claims data for step therapy.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; API-USAGE-METRICS; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; GENERAL
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** 42 CFR Part 2.
- **Standards referenced:** Prior Authorization API, Patient Access API, Provider Access API, Payer-to-Payer API, NCPDP standards, historical claims data, automated adjudication tools.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Drug PA turnaround times and stop-the-clock policy**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** ABHW argues pharmacy PAs often involve dosage limits, quantity limits, step therapy, site-of-care issues, diagnosis-specific criteria, and documentation needs that cannot always be resolved within shortened deadlines.
- **Specific request:** Allow plans to pause turnaround-time requirements when clinically necessary information has been requested but not yet received.

**Topic 2: Bundled behavioral health and SUD services**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL
- **Position:** Clarify / Modify
- **Rationale:** Some behavioral health Medicaid MCOs cover MAT through bundled case rates that include medication plus counseling, labs, assessments, and other services, making classification as a drug PA operationally difficult.
- **Specific request:** Exempt bundled BH/SUD treatment services that include medications from the 24-hour drug PA timeframe and process them under non-drug PA API requirements and non-drug timeframes.

**Topic 3: NCPDP versus Prior Authorization API classification**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Clarify
- **Rationale:** ABHW states bundled MAT services are broader than pharmacy benefit transactions and may require credentialing and service review.
- **Specific request:** Clarify that bundled services are processed through the Prior Authorization API for non-drug items and services, not NCPDP pharmacy-benefit standards.

**Topic 4: Payer-to-payer privacy limits**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** ABHW is concerned broad payer-to-payer exchange of structured and unstructured clinical documentation could disclose unnecessary sensitive behavioral health information, including Part 2-protected information.
- **Specific request:** Limit payer-to-payer exchange to active plan transitions, require explicit member authorization, and restrict data to the minimum necessary.

**Topic 5: Step therapy data sharing**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Historical claims can reduce duplicative therapy requirements for new members, but payer criteria differ based on clinical policies, formularies, and benefit designs.
- **Specific request:** Support targeted historical claims use while preserving payer flexibility and avoiding automatic acceptance of other payers' step therapy determinations.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S14:** ABHW requests clarification of when NCPDP pharmacy standards apply, specifically asking that bundled BH/SUD services be handled through the non-drug Prior Authorization API rather than NCPDP standards.
- **S20:** ABHW argues 24-hour drug PA timeframes may be operationally unrealistic for complex pharmacy reviews and asks for a stop-the-clock mechanism.
- **S43:** ABHW addresses alignment of drug and non-drug timeframes by requesting non-drug PA timeframes for bundled services that include medications but also broader clinical services.
- **S30:** ABHW raises privacy concerns about broad payer-to-payer exchange, especially for behavioral health and 42 CFR Part 2 information, and requests explicit member authorization and minimum necessary limits.
- **S66-S82:** ABHW responds to the step therapy RFI by supporting targeted historical claims data use for new members while opposing mandatory acceptance of other payers' determinations.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Allow plans to stop the PA turnaround clock when additional clinically necessary information has been requested but not received.
2. Exempt bundled behavioral health and SUD treatment services that include medications from 24-hour drug PA timeframes.
3. Apply non-drug PA timeframes of 7 calendar days standard and 72 hours expedited to bundled BH/SUD services.
4. Clarify bundled BH/SUD services should use the non-drug Prior Authorization API rather than NCPDP pharmacy-benefit standards.
5. Limit payer-to-payer data exchange to active transitions where data are needed for continuity of care.
6. Require explicit member authorization before payer-to-payer exchange of sensitive information.
7. Apply minimum necessary limits and avoid transmission of full clinical documentation when targeted data will suffice.
8. Support targeted historical claims use for step therapy, especially for new members.
9. Preserve payer flexibility to apply plan-specific clinical criteria and avoid automatic acceptance of another payer's step therapy decision.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Unrealistic timeframes for complex pharmacy PAs, increased denials from incomplete requests, operational burden for bundled BH/SUD services, sensitive behavioral health data disclosure, and loss of payer flexibility in step therapy.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** More denials, appeals, administrative burden, delayed patient access, compliance challenges, privacy breaches, and undermined program integrity safeguards.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** System changes, workflow redesign, technology investments, pharmacy benefit complexity, credentialing needs, bundled payment measurement issues, and Part 2 confidentiality requirements.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** ABHW states its member companies cover 200 million people.
- **Studies or research referenced:** Not addressed.
- **Examples provided:** Louisiana Medicaid opioid treatment program bundled payment for HCPCS code H0020, including methadone dosing/dispensing, counseling, urine drug testing, physician exams, evaluation and management visits, care coordination, and labs.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Behavioral health payers, Medicaid managed care organizations, PBMs, providers, opioid treatment programs, patients receiving MAT or behavioral health services, state Medicaid programs, and members transitioning between plans.
- **Economic implications:** ABHW anticipates significant system, workflow, and technology investments, plus costs from denials, appeals, and administrative rework if timeframes are too rigid.
- **Technical feasibility:** ABHW supports electronic PA and historical claims data use but warns implementation must reflect complex pharmacy and bundled-service workflows.
- **Patient care impact:** Mixed; faster PA can improve access, but rigid deadlines or broad data sharing could increase denials, delay care, or compromise privacy.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Mixed; supportive of goals but concerned about operational feasibility and privacy.
- **Tone:** Professional, technical, and pragmatic.
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "The proposed turnaround times do not adequately account for the clinical and operational complexity" - Context: ABHW's objection to shortened pharmacy PA deadlines.
2. "allow health plans to pause applicable turnaround time requirements" - Context: Specific stop-the-clock recommendation.
3. "bundled behavioral health and SUD treatment services that include medications be exempt" - Context: Request for bundled service treatment under non-drug rules.
4. "require explicit member authorization before information is shared" - Context: Privacy recommendation for payer-to-payer exchange.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - ABHW objects to short PA turnaround deadlines without stop-the-clock flexibility.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - The comment cites system changes, workflow redesign, technology investments, denials, appeals, and administrative burden.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - It warns incomplete requests and bundled service complexity could increase burden for providers and plans.
- [x] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - The comment raises behavioral health and 42 CFR Part 2 confidentiality concerns in payer-to-payer exchange.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - The comment focuses on mental health, SUD, MAT, and whole-person behavioral health access.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - ABHW supports electronic PA but asks CMS to account for operational complexity and historical claims data capabilities.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Recommendations are framed around avoiding denials, appeals, delays, and privacy harms while preserving continuity of care.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - The bundled MAT discussion directly concerns whether services should be treated as drug/pharmacy or non-drug medical PA.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - ABHW asks CMS to preserve payer-specific criteria, transition-of-care mechanisms, grandfathering, and override processes.
